I heard a discussion with screenwriter Max Landis (son of John Landis) in which he commented that Hollywood is very concerned about this question.

As a guy who is probably a bit older than many of you, my concept of "movie star" is going to be a lot different. Real movie stars used to be folks whose very name on the marquee would command a large audience. And folks who attained this "star" status generally had decades-long careers marked by big films that were often also critically acclaimed. Folks like Robert Redford, Paul Newman, John Wayne come to mind. More recent examples would be Tom Hanks, Brad Pitt, and Tom Cruise. There are lots of other "stars" who have taken a different path and begun to cash in on their name by doing direct-to-video crap...folks like Robert DeNero, Al Pacino, Bruce Willis, et.al. Folks like Robert Downey Jr. might be considered, but he's no spring chicken. Maybe Bradley Cooper--but do people really go to see a "Bradley Cooper movie?"

Obviously we do have some actors who still achieve great notoriety, but with the decline/change of cinema I'm not sure if any of them will ever achieve the type of "stardom" of their predecessors. Let me be clear, I'm not disparaging the actors themselves--only questioning whether or not Hollywood is still capable of producing big "movie stars."
Will there ever be new "movie stars" again?

There will be movie stars, but fewer of them. Hollywood has changed significantly from the days when studios could groom an actor to the point where he or she was a marketable commodity. And that is what movie stars are: commodities. Even Cary Grant said he wished he could be Cary Grant.

Besides the packaging of actors, there is also a change in movie goers tastes. I'm not sure movie goers desire the glamor of old Hollywood anymore. Maybe it has to do with anti-elitist feelings coinciding with a struggling economy, but social media has made it possible to knock any up and coming actor off his or her pedestal the minute fans get a sense that they are being "sold" on the latest flavor of the month.

There is also the economics of the movie business. Multi million dollar movies that aim for block buster status seem to emphasize special effects over acting talent, which further diminishes the possibility of breeding a large pool of movie stars.

I don't disagree with you, but who are these newer actors who will become stars? I could name a bunch of "big names" (e.g. Channing Tatum), but none of them really seem like they're destined to being anything more than a leading man as opposed to a movie star like Tom Hanks or Tom Cruise. Again, don't get me wrong--I'm not bashing the actors, but like you said, it's unclear if the Hollywood system is capable of producing real stars anymore...hence the post. I'd love to hear any names folks think might eventually get there.

I think I understand what you are saying. Perhaps we should distinguish between a movie star (someone who appears in high gross films) and actors (someone who people will see for their skills and talent).

By this definition, someone like Ben Stiller would be considered a movie star while Daniel Day Lewis would be considered an actor.

In this case, movie stars are measured by economics and are therefore created accidentally while actors are measured by their devotion to craft. It is entirely possible for a talented actor to be a movie star, but less likely that a movie star will be widely considered a talented actor.

Of course these terms are prone to melt into each other and the issue you raise becomes more complicated when you introduce the question of taste.

For instance, I think Bradley Cooper is a good actor, and he has demonstrated that he is a decent leading man. His performance in American Sniper hints that he can carry a movie, but is he a movie star? That seems to be a question that can be answered by looking at his box office. Meanwhile I think Seth Rogan is an abysmal actor, a pox on the acting profession, but his movies make money and so Hollywood considers him a star.

To me, a "movie star" is someone whose name is bankable and whose influence and box-office appeal stretches across at least 2 decades. Tom Hanks, Brad Pitt, and Tom Cruise are three that I would 100% identify as current movie stars. Any of those guys could get any project greenlighted, and any film with them in it is going to illicit a lot of interest (both in the US and worldwide). Folks like DeNero, Pacino, and Bruce Willis used to be in that category, but their influence and appeal have sharply diminished.

You bring up an interesting case with Seth Rogan. Lots of people will go see a film if he's in it. He's had success at the box office, but none of it has commanded any real critical acclaim so I wouldn't bank on him ever attaining "movie star" status.

I probably should have mentioned Clint Eastwood. He's had an astonishing film career that has spanned over 5 decades and even the films he directs have command lots of acclaim. The only current actor remotely following in his footsteps is Ben Affleck, but his movies have been pretty hit or miss. However, he did win an Oscar for writing, and he received lots of praise for directing Argo so he might have some lasting power. But then again, he's been a known quantity since the 90s, so he's not exactly an up-and-coming actor.

Most movies now are made for global audiences - actors are overdubbed, plots are simplistic and easy to restructure (ie, for Chinese censors).
